content.title: About
content.content: Barbecue pork with sauce consists of tender pork pieces marinated in spices and slowly grilled, served with a sweet‑tangy sauce. The dish is popular in American and European cuisines, combining the smoky flavor of the meat with a rich, flavorful sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional barbecue sauce is often made from tomato paste, vinegar, brown sugar, and spices.
Pork is considered more tender than beef due to its higher fat content, making it ideal for long‑time smoking.
In the United States, over 50 million pounds of barbecue sauce are consumed each year.
Regional sauce variations exist: North Carolina favors a vinegar‑based sauce, while Texas prefers a thicker tomato‑based version.
Barbecue pork is commonly served with coleslaw, cornbread, or mashed potatoes.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Pork provides complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin source
items.content: It contains thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are important for immune function and blood formation.

items.title: Polyunsaturated fats in the sauce
items.content: When the sauce is made with vegetable oils, it can add beneficial omega‑6 fatty acids.

items.title: Antioxidants from spices
items.content: Garlic, paprika, and mustard powder contain compounds with antioxidant properties.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Barbecue sauces often contain a lot of salt, which may raise blood pressure if consumed in excess.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet sauces can contribute to elevated blood glucose levels.

items.title: Fat overconsumption
items.content: Fatty pork can increase the calorie density of the meal.

items.title: Allergy to spices
items.content: Some individuals may react to mustard, garlic, or other sauce ingredients.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the barbecue pork hot, sliced into portions. It pairs well with cornbread, baked potatoes, fresh vegetable salads, or coleslaw. Add extra sauce to taste if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked pork in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. The sauce can be frozen in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 74 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Salmon fillet NFS (1084) is fresh, ocean-caught salmon harvested from the pristine waters of the North Pacific. The flesh is bright pink, tender, and carries a distinct sea aroma. It is suitable for baking, pan‑frying, grilling, and steaming.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Salmon are one of the few fish that migrate from the ocean to freshwater rivers to spawn.
In the wild, salmon can live up to 7 years, with some individuals reaching 20 years.
Salmon meat is rich in omega‑3 fatty acids, which are important for cardiovascular health.
NFS (No Further Specification) indicates the product has no additional restrictions regarding farming or processing methods.
Salmon has long been a delicacy in Scandinavian and Japanese cuisines.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Salmon provides EPA and DHA, long‑chain omega‑3s that help lower triglycerides and support brain function.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A 100 g serving delivers about 20 g of complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Salmon is a good source of B12, B6, and niacin, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant and supports the immune system.

items.title: Vitamin D
items.content: Salmon is one of the few natural food sources of vitamin D, important for bone health.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including salmon.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: While salmon generally has low mercury levels, moderate consumption is advised, especially for pregnant women and children.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Improper storage or insufficient cooking can allow bacterial growth.

items.title: Environmental contaminants
items.content: Occasionally, trace amounts of PCBs and dioxins may be present in fish.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Salmon fillet can be baked at 180 °C for 12‑15 minutes, pan‑seared 3‑4 minutes per side, grilled, or steamed. Before cooking, remove the skin if desired, lightly season with salt, and add lemon juice or herbs for flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store salmon fillet in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C in an airtight container for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 3 months. Before use, check for a fresh sea scent; avoid any strong, sour, or off‑putting odors.
